title: The CF Connection: Extended GCD = Continued Fraction Algorithm
content: The preamble explains why divisibility osculators and continued fractions are connected: the Euclidean algorithm for gcd(10, d) produces the same sequence of quotients as the CF expansion of 10/d, and the Bézout coefficients (gcdA(10,d), gcdB(10,d)) equal the numerator and denominator of the last convergent. However — and this is the key insight of the file — the existential conclusion (a natural-number osculator in [0,d) exists) follows from Bézout alone, without constructing the CF expansion. The CF framing is conceptually illuminating but not formally required for this particular statement.
mathContext: The CF expansion of $10/d$: $10/d = q_0 + 1/(q_1 + 1/(q_2 + \cdots))$ where $q_k$ are the Euclidean quotients from $\gcd(10, d)$. The last convergent denominator equals $\gcd A(10, d)$, confirming that the osculator is a convergent denominator. But for existence, only $\gcd A(10, d) \bmod d \in [0, d)$ is needed.

title: Bézout Identity Directly Gives the Osculator
content: `bezout_gives_osculator` extracts the osculator from Mathlib's `Nat.gcd_eq_gcd_ab` identity: `gcd(10,d) = 10·gcdA(10,d) + d·gcdB(10,d)`. When `gcd(10,d) = 1` (i.e., d coprime to 10), this gives `1 = 10·gcdA(10,d) + d·gcdB(10,d)`, rearranging to `d | 10·gcdA(10,d) − 1`. The proof uses `linear_combination -hbez` to close the divisibility goal. This is the key observation: the osculator IS the Bézout coefficient, no further construction needed.
mathContext: The modular inverse of 10 mod d is exactly `gcdA(10,d) mod d`. The Bézout identity certifies this directly: if $1 = 10a + db$, then $10a \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, so $a$ is the inverse and $d \mid 10a - 1$.

title: Osculator Uniqueness via Coprimality: IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left
content: `osculator_unique_mod` shows any two osculators c, c' satisfy `d | c − c'`. Proof: if `d | 10c − 1` and `d | 10c' − 1`, then `d | 10(c − c')`. Since `gcd(10,d) = 1` (coprimality), `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` gives `d | c − c'`. This is the crucial coprimality cancellation: `gcd(10,d) = 1` allows removing the factor 10 from the divisibility.
mathContext: In a UFD (or any integral domain), if $a \mid bc$ and $\gcd(a,b) = 1$, then $a \mid c$. Here: $d \mid 10(c-c')$ and $\gcd(d,10) = 1$ (note: symmetry of coprimality is used via `.symm`) gives $d \mid (c-c')$.

title: Canonical Osculator: Reduction Mod d and Uniqueness
content: Part III establishes that the canonical representative `gcdA(10,d) % d` is the unique osculator in [0,d). Three lemmas: (1) `osculator_mod_d_is_osculator`: the reduced value is still an osculator (proved via `osculator_congr`, which says osculators in the same residue class are all osculators); (2) `osculator_mod_d_bounded`: the reduced value has |·| < d (from `Int.emod_nonneg` and `Int.emod_lt_of_pos`); (3) `canonical_osculator_unique`: every osculator c satisfies d | c − (gcdA mod d), proved by combining two applications of `osculator_unique_mod` and adding the divisibilities via `dvd_add`. The proof uses `Int.ediv_add_emod` (the integer division identity n = (n/d)·d + n%d) to verify the congruence condition.
mathContext: The canonical osculator is $c_0 = \gcd A(10,d) \bmod d \in [0,d)$. Every osculator $c$ satisfies $d \mid c - c_0$ (i.e., $c \equiv c_0 \pmod{d}$). This makes $c_0$ the unique representative of the modular inverse of 10 in $\{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}$.

title: Existential Proof Without Continued Fractions
content: `cf_bezout_correspondence` was originally planned as ~200 lines connecting `GenContFract` and `Nat.xgcd`. The actual proof is ~20 lines: (1) `n₀ := gcdA(10,d) % d` is a non-negative integer in [0,d) (by `Int.emod_nonneg` and `Int.emod_lt_of_pos`); (2) it is still an osculator (by `osculator_mod_d_is_osculator`); (3) `Int.toNat n₀` is the ℕ witness. The `refine ⟨n₀.toNat, ?_, ?_⟩` pattern splits into the bound `n₀.toNat < d` and the osculator property. `omega` closes the bound after casting back via `Int.toNat_of_nonneg`.
mathContext: The existential $\exists n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < d \wedge d \mid 10n - 1$ does not require knowing WHICH convergent of $10/d$ equals $n$. It only needs: a valid osculator exists, and it can be reduced to $[0,d)$. The CF connection is informative but not proof-essential for this particular statement.

title: Concrete Divisibility Tests: d = 7, 11, 13, 19
content: Five concrete examples instantiate the general theory: `osculator_seven : IsOsculator 7 (−2)` means 7 | 10·(−2) − 1 = −21, checked by `norm_num`. The corresponding divisibility test `div_by_seven`: `7 | n ↔ 7 | (n/10) − 2·(n%10)` applies `unified_osculator` from OQ-01. The d=11 case (c=−1) gives the classical alternating digit sum rule. Each osculator is verified by `norm_num` after unfolding `IsOsculator`.
mathContext: Concrete osculators: $7 \leftrightarrow -2$ (or $+5$), $11 \leftrightarrow -1$ (alternating digit sum), $13 \leftrightarrow 4$, $17 \leftrightarrow -5$, $19 \leftrightarrow 2$. These are precisely the values of $\gcd A(10,d) \bmod d$ for each $d$, confirming the general theorem.
